claim: The 'neural plate border' of vertebrate embryos contains precursors of neural crest and placode cells.
source: The 'neural plate border' of vertebrate embryos contains precursors of neural crest and placode cells, both defining vertebrate characteristics.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a foundational premise of the study.

claim: Neural crest and placode cells are defining vertebrate characteristics.
source: The 'neural plate border' of vertebrate embryos contains precursors of neural crest and placode cells, both defining vertebrate characteristics.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is established scientific knowledge.

claim: Individual border cells show significant overlap of transcription factors characteristic of multiple lineages from gastrula through neurula stages.
source: The results reveal significant overlap of transcription factors characteristic of multiple lineages in individual border cells from gastrula through neurula stages.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by quantitative analysis throughout the manuscript.

claim: Cells that are initially Sox2+ can contribute to neural tube, neural crest, and epidermis.
source: Cell fate analysis using a Sox2 (neural) enhancer reveals that cells that are initially Sox2+ cells can contribute not only to neural tube but also to neural crest and epidermis.
evidence: This is a primary finding from cell fate analysis experiments described in the abstract and Results section.

claim: Modulating levels of Sox2 or Pax7 alters the apportionment of neural tube versus neural crest fates.
source: Moreover, modulating levels of Sox2 or Pax7 alters the apportionment of neural tube versus neural crest fates.
evidence: This is a primary finding from gain- and loss-of-function experiments described in the abstract and Results section.

claim: Many individual border cells maintain ability to contribute to multiple ectodermal lineages until or beyond neural tube closure.
source: Our results resolve a long-standing question and suggest that many individual border cells maintain ability to contribute to multiple ectodermal lineages until or beyond neural tube closure.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract, supported by the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Neural crest cells differentiate into sensory and autonomic ganglia, pigment cells and elements of the craniofacial skeleton.
source: Neural crest cells differentiate into sensory and autonomic ganglia, pigment cells and elements of the craniofacial skeleton, whereas ectodermal placodes give rise to the ear, nose, lens and sensory ganglia of the head.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge stated in the Introduction.

claim: Ectodermal placodes give rise to the ear, nose, lens and sensory ganglia of the head.
source: Neural crest cells differentiate into sensory and autonomic ganglia, pigment cells and elements of the craniofacial skeleton, whereas ectodermal placodes give rise to the ear, nose, lens and sensory ganglia of the head.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge stated in the Introduction.

claim: Neural crest and placode cells originate from a region of ectoderm at the juncture between neural and non-neural ectoderm, the 'neural plate border'.
source: In vertebrates, neural crest and placode cells originate from a region of ectoderm at the juncture between neural and non-neural ectoderm, the 'neural plate border'.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge stated in the Introduction.

claim: Basal chordate embryos possess a sharp demarcation between presumptive neural and epidermal fates at the neural plate border.
source: Whereas basal chordate embryos possess a sharp demarcation between presumptive neural and epidermal fates at this border, much less in known about how cell fates as disparate as neural crest, placode and CNS cells become segregated at the neural plate border of vertebrate embryos.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction as established knowledge about basal chordates.

claim: The classical view is that the vertebrate neural plate border initially contains intermingled precursors of various fates that by neurula stages become subdivided into separate zones.
source: The classical view, favored in many reviews and textbooks, is that the vertebrate neural plate border initially contains intermingled precursors of various fates that by neurula stages become subdivided into separate zones, with placodal precursors found more laterally and neural crest precursors more medially (Groves and LaBonne, 2014; Moody and LaMantia, 2015; Patthey and Gunhaga, 2011; Saint-Jeannet and Moody, 2014; Streit, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple review articles and textbooks.

claim: In the classical view, placodal precursors are found more laterally and neural crest precursors more medially by neurula stages.
source: The classical view, favored in many reviews and textbooks, is that the vertebrate neural plate border initially contains intermingled precursors of various fates that by neurula stages become subdivided into separate zones, with placodal precursors found more laterally and neural crest precursors more medially (Groves and LaBonne, 2014; Moody and LaMantia, 2015; Patthey and Gunhaga, 2011; Saint-Jeannet and Moody, 2014; Streit, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple review articles.

claim: Focal injections of DiI in gastrula stage chicken embryos result in DiI-labeled cells localized to multiple tissues (e.g. epidermis, neural tube, neural crest and placode).
source: In past decades, this question has been addressed by fate mapping studies in which small groups of neural plate border (Schoenwolf and Sheard, 1990) or presumptive placodal precursors (Streit, 2002) were labeled using focal injections of the lipophilic dye DiI in gastrula stage chicken embryos. This results in DiI-labeled cells localized to multiple tissues (e.g. epidermis, neural tube, neural crest and placode).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous fate mapping studies.

claim: DiI labeling typically labels small numbers (10-50) of cells.
source: However, DiI labeling typically labels small numbers (10-50) of cells, thus leaving open the question of whether the neural plate border contains multipotent and/or intermixed, fate restricted cells and their relative positions.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of previous DiI labeling studies.

claim: Single cell lineage tracing has been performed in the trunk neural crest just prior to their emigration.
source: While single cell lineage tracing has partially addressed this issue in the trunk neural crest just prior to their emigration (Baggiolini et al., 2015; Bronner-Fraser and Fraser, 1988; McKinney et al., 2013), these studies did not examine early neural plate border stages or the relationship between different transcription factors in the border region.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous single cell lineage tracing studies.

claim: Previous single cell lineage tracing studies did not examine early neural plate border stages or the relationship between different transcription factors in the border region.
source: While single cell lineage tracing has partially addressed this issue in the trunk neural crest just prior to their emigration (Baggiolini et al., 2015; Bronner-Fraser and Fraser, 1988; McKinney et al., 2013), these studies did not examine early neural plate border stages or the relationship between different transcription factors in the border region.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in previous research that the current study addresses.

claim: Sox2 is expressed throughout the neural plate at mid- to late gastrula stages (HH4 to HH4+).
source: Here, we define the neural plate border at mid- to late gastrula stages (HH4 to HH4+) by virtue of the expression of Sox2 throughout the neural plate and Tfap2a, which is expressed throughout the presumptive non-neural ectoderm at this stage.
evidence: This is stated as a defining characteristic used in the study.

claim: Tfap2a is expressed throughout the presumptive non-neural ectoderm at mid- to late gastrula stages (HH4 to HH4+).
source: Here, we define the neural plate border at mid- to late gastrula stages (HH4 to HH4+) by virtue of the expression of Sox2 throughout the neural plate and Tfap2a, which is expressed throughout the presumptive non-neural ectoderm at this stage.
evidence: This is stated as a defining characteristic used in the study.

claim: Pax7 is one of the earliest markers of the neural plate border.
source: At subsequent stages, we use Pax7 to define the extent of the border, since it is one of the earliest markers of the neural plate border and becomes quickly restricted to this region (Basch et al., 2006; Khudyakov and Bronner-Fraser, 2009; Otto et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Pax7 becomes quickly restricted to the neural plate border region.
source: At subsequent stages, we use Pax7 to define the extent of the border, since it is one of the earliest markers of the neural plate border and becomes quickly restricted to this region (Basch et al., 2006; Khudyakov and Bronner-Fraser, 2009; Otto et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Neural tube closure occurs at HH8+ in the cranial region.
source: With time, the neural plate border elevates to form the neural folds as the embryo undergoes neurulation until the time of neural tube closure at HH8+ in the cranial region.
evidence: This is stated as a developmental timing fact.

claim: Neural crest emigration from the neural tube commences at HH9.
source: Neural crest emigration from the neural tube then commences at HH9.
evidence: This is stated as a developmental timing fact.

claim: Cells coexpressing Tfap2a and Sox2 can be observed as early as HH4+.
source: We observe cells coexpressing Tfap2a and Sox2 as early as HH4+ (Figure 1B) and continuing through later stages, e.g. at HH8 and HH10 (Figure 1C and D), at which time we also observe concomitant expression of Sox2, Pax7 and Tfap2a in individual neural plate border cells.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Concomitant expression of Sox2, Pax7 and Tfap2a occurs in individual neural plate border cells at HH8 and HH10.
source: We observe cells coexpressing Tfap2a and Sox2 as early as HH4+ (Figure 1B) and continuing through later stages, e.g. at HH8 and HH10 (Figure 1C and D), at which time we also observe concomitant expression of Sox2, Pax7 and Tfap2a in individual neural plate border cells.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figures 1C and D.

claim: Cells co-expressing Msx1/2 and Sox2 can be observed at HH6 to HH10.
source: Similarly, cells co-expressing Msx1/2 and Sox2 can be observed at HH6 to HH10 (Figure 1E–H).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figures 1E-H.

claim: Co-expression of Msx1/2 with the placodal marker Six1 can be observed at HH8 in the dorsal neural folds.
source: Co-expression of Msx1/2 with the placodal marker Six1 as well as Six1 plus Sox2 can be observed at HH8 in the dorsal neural folds (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Co-expression of Six1 plus Sox2 can be observed at HH8 in the dorsal neural folds.
source: Co-expression of Msx1/2 with the placodal marker Six1 as well as Six1 plus Sox2 can be observed at HH8 in the dorsal neural folds (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: At HH10, coexpression of Sox2, Msx1/2 and Six1 is only observed in the ectoderm since Six1 is no longer expressed in the neural crest or dorsal neural tube by this stage.
source: At HH10, however, coexpression of Sox2, Msx1/2 and Six1 is only observed in the ectoderm since Six1 is no longer expressed in the neural crest or dorsal neural tube by this stage (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Expression of Sox2 extends throughout the entire neural plate border region when compared with Msx1/2 and Pax7 at all time points examined.
source: Interestingly, in addition to the neural plate territory, expression of Sox2 extends throughout the entire neural plate border region when compared with Msx1/2 and Pax7 at all time points examined (Figure 1C–H).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figures 1C-H.

claim: Some cells only express a single marker at a time at all stages, though this appears to be a minority population.
source: Nevertheless, we do also observe some cells that only express a single marker at a time at all stages, though this appears to be a minority population.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the immunostaining data.

claim: ~70% of all cells at the neural plate border express Sox2 at HH5.
source: Our coexpression analyses show that ~70% of all cells at the neural plate border express Sox2 and about 75% express Pax7 (Figure 2F and G) at HH5.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2F.

claim: About 75% of all cells at the neural plate border express Pax7 at HH5.
source: Our coexpression analyses show that ~70% of all cells at the neural plate border express Sox2 and about 75% express Pax7 (Figure 2F and G) at HH5.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2G.

claim: About 44% of neural plate border cells coexpress Sox2/Pax7 at HH5.
source: However, more than half of these cells (~44%) coexpress Sox2/Pax7 at HH5, which rises significantly to about 54% at HH6 and remains relatively constant until HH9 (~58%) (Figure 2I).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2I.

claim: Sox2/Pax7 coexpression rises significantly to about 54% at HH6.
source: However, more than half of these cells (~44%) coexpress Sox2/Pax7 at HH5, which rises significantly to about 54% at HH6 and remains relatively constant until HH9 (~58%) (Figure 2I).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2I.

claim: Sox2/Pax7 coexpression remains relatively constant at about 58% until HH9.
source: However, more than half of these cells (~44%) coexpress Sox2/Pax7 at HH5, which rises significantly to about 54% at HH6 and remains relatively constant until HH9 (~58%) (Figure 2I).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2I.

claim: Cells coexpressing Sox2/Six1, but not Pax7 ranged between 0–1%.
source: Cells coexpressing Sox2/Six1, but not Pax7 ranged between 0–1%, and cells coexpressing Six1/Pax7 but not Sox2 between 1% (HH6) and 4% (HH9) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–D and F).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Cells coexpressing Six1/Pax7 but not Sox2 ranged between 1% (HH6) and 4% (HH9).
source: Cells coexpressing Sox2/Six1, but not Pax7 ranged between 0–1%, and cells coexpressing Six1/Pax7 but not Sox2 between 1% (HH6) and 4% (HH9) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–D and F).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Cells coexpressing all three markers (Sox2, Pax7 and Six1) peaked at 7% at HH8.
source: However, cells coexpressing all three markers (Sox2, Pax7 and Six1) peaked at 7% at HH8 (Figure 2J).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2J.

claim: There is a higher degree of coexpression of Sox2, Pax7 and Tfap2a.
source: Similarly, we see a higher degree of coexpression of Sox2, Pax7 and Tfap2a (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1G.

claim: There is a burst of triple marker coexpression between HH7 to HH8.
source: These data indicate a burst of triple marker coexpression between HH7 to HH8.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the quantitative data showing peak coexpression at HH8.

claim: 23–24% of the cells express Sox2 alone at HH5-6.
source: For example, 23–24% of the cells express Sox2 alone at HH5-6 (Figure 2F'').
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2F''.

claim: The percentage of cells expressing Sox2 alone significantly decreases to about 13–14% at HH8-9.
source: Although one might expect that this number would increase with time as an indication that cells are becoming progressively restricted, instead we find that this number significantly decreases to about 13–14% at HH8-9 (Figure 2F'').
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2F''.

claim: 26% of the cells express Pax7 alone at HH5.
source: In the case of Pax7, 26% of the cells express Pax7 alone at HH5 and this significantly decreases to 18% and 12% at HH6 and HH8, respectively, before it slightly increases again at HH9% to 17% (Figure 2G''), possibly indicating the onset of neural crest migration.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2G''.

claim: Pax7-only expression significantly decreases to 18% and 12% at HH6 and HH8, respectively.
source: In the case of Pax7, 26% of the cells express Pax7 alone at HH5 and this significantly decreases to 18% and 12% at HH6 and HH8, respectively, before it slightly increases again at HH9% to 17% (Figure 2G''), possibly indicating the onset of neural crest migration.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2G''.

claim: Pax7-only expression slightly increases again at HH9 to 17%, possibly indicating the onset of neural crest migration.
source: In the case of Pax7, 26% of the cells express Pax7 alone at HH5 and this significantly decreases to 18% and 12% at HH6 and HH8, respectively, before it slightly increases again at HH9% to 17% (Figure 2G''), possibly indicating the onset of neural crest migration.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2G'' and is a speculative interpretation.

claim: Six1 is expressed alone in about 1% and 3% of the cells at HH5/6 and HH8/9, respectively.
source: Six1 is expressed alone in about 1% and 3% of the cells at HH5/6 and HH8/9, respectively (Figure 2H'').
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2H''.

claim: Roughly double the number of cells express two or more markers when compared to cells expressing only one of the three markers at a time.
source: Altogether, this quantitative analysis shows that roughly double the number of cells express two or more markers when compared to cells expressing only one of the three markers at a time (Figure 2K).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2K.

claim: The percentage of cells co-expressing different transcription factors increases over time while the number of cells expressing individual markers within the neural plate border diminishes.
source: Moreover, the percentage of cells co-expressing different transcription factors increases over time while the number of cells expressing individual markers within the neural plate border diminishes, contrary to what would be expected if the developmental potential of cells was decreasing with time.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the quantitative data presented in Figure 2.

claim: The neural plate border narrows over time, such that at HH5 Pax7 expression at the neural plate border is wider than at later stages of development.
source: We found that the neural plate border narrows over time, such that at HH5 Pax7 expression at the neural plate border is wider than at later stages of development (Figure 3G–I).
evidence: This is supported by intensity profile analysis shown in Figures 3G-I.

claim: The intensity of Pax7 expression increases over time between HH5 to HH6.
source: Similarly, the intensity of Pax7 expression increases over time between HH5 to HH6 (Figure 3G–H).
evidence: This is supported by intensity profile analysis shown in Figures 3G-H.

claim: There is no significant increase of Pax7 expression within the dorsal neural fold between HH8 and HH9.
source: Within the dorsal neural fold, there is no significant increase of Pax7 expression between HH8 (5–9 sections/embryo, n = 7 embryos) and HH9 (3–6 sections/embryo, n = 5 embryos), but Pax7 expression increases significantly in the delaminating neural crest, which could indicate a time point of fate determination at this stage (Figure 3J).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3J.

claim: Pax7 expression increases significantly in the delaminating neural crest between HH8 and HH9, which could indicate a time point of fate determination at this stage.
source: Within the dorsal neural fold, there is no significant increase of Pax7 expression between HH8 (5–9 sections/embryo, n = 7 embryos) and HH9 (3–6 sections/embryo, n = 5 embryos), but Pax7 expression increases significantly in the delaminating neural crest, which could indicate a time point of fate determination at this stage (Figure 3J).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3J and includes a speculative interpretation.

claim: Sox2 intensity profile remains relatively constant over time between HH5 and HH8.
source: Next, we assessed how Sox2 expression changes over time. Sox2 intensity profile remains relatively constant over time between HH5 and HH8 (Figure 3G–I).
evidence: This is supported by intensity profile analysis shown in Figures 3G-I.

claim: Between HH8 and HH9, Sox2 expression in the dorsal neural fold changes significantly and then drops again in neural crest cells that have delaminated from the neural tube.
source: However, between HH8 and HH9, Sox2 expression in the dorsal neural fold changes significantly and then drops again in neural crest cells that have delaminated from the neural tube (Figure 3J).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3J.

claim: At HH10 Sox2 expression is maintained in the dorsal neural tube even as neural crest cells begin to migrate away.
source: At HH10 Sox2 expression is maintained in the dorsal neural tube even as neural crest cells begin to migrate away (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Sox2/Six1 double and Sox2/Six1/Pax7 triple positive cells are found in the epidermis at HH10.
source: Interestingly, we also find Sox2/Six1 double and Sox2/Six1/Pax7 triple positive cells in the epidermis (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Pax7 positive cells in the dorsal neural tube still express Sox2 at HH11 and HH12 even though most of the neural crest cells have already migrated away from the dorsal region.
source: When immunostaining HH11 and HH12 embryos for Sox2 expression, we find that Pax7 positive cells in the dorsal neural tube still express Sox2 even though most of the neural crest cells have already migrated away from the dorsal region (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figures 4B and C.

claim: Low levels of Sox2 can be observed in early and late migrating neural crest cells.
source: Low levels of Sox2 can also be observed in early and late migrating neural crest cells(Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figures 4B and C.

claim: From medial to lateral, Pax7 is most medial, followed by Tfap2a, then Msx1/2 with Six1 being lateral-most.
source: In comparing the spatial distribution of transcription factors at the neural plate border from medial to lateral, Pax7 is most medial, followed by Tfap2a, then Msx1/2 with Six1 being lateral-most (Figure 3K–M and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by intensity profile analysis shown in Figures 3K-M and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: There is an area on the lateral side of the neural plate border where the expression of all these transcription factors overlaps.
source: However, there is an area on the lateral side of the neural plate border where the expression of all these transcription factors overlaps, suggesting that there are cells that potentially express all five markers simultaneously.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the intensity profile data shown in Figures 3K-M.

claim: The N1 and N2 Sox2 enhancers drive reporter expression in a manner that recapitulates endogenous Sox2 gene expression only in the neural plate and neural tube.
source: For this purpose, we used the well characterized N1 and N2 Sox2 enhancers to drive reporter expression in a manner that recapitulates endogenous Sox2 gene expression only in the neural plate and neural tube (Uchikawa et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study characterizing these enhancers.

claim: eGFP protein has a half-life of approximately 26 hr in mammalian cells.
source: eGFP protein is highly stable and has a half-life of approximately 26 hr in mammalian cells (Corish and Tyler-Smith, 1999); addition of a H2B nuclear localization signal has been reported to further stabilize the fluorescent label (Foudi et al., 2009; Kanda et al., 1998), making it an advantageous tool to trace cell fates.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Addition of a H2B nuclear localization signal has been reported to further stabilize the fluorescent label.
source: eGFP protein is highly stable and has a half-life of approximately 26 hr in mammalian cells (Corish and Tyler-Smith, 1999); addition of a H2B nuclear localization signal has been reported to further stabilize the fluorescent label (Foudi et al., 2009; Kanda et al., 1998), making it an advantageous tool to trace cell fates.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The N1 and N2 Sox2 enhancers do not drive expression in the neural crest.
source: Because these enhancers do not drive expression in the neural crest (Uchikawa et al., 2003), we were able to follow the contributions of cells that initially express Sox2 to embryonic tissues (e.g. neural tube, neural crest, and/or ectoderm) at later times.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The first eGFP protein signal is visible 3 hr post electroporation of the N1N2-H2BeGFP Sox2-reporter.
source: After introduction of the N1N2-H2BeGFP Sox2-reporter into HH3-4 embryos, the first eGFP protein signal is visible 3 hr post electroporation.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiments.

claim: The N1N2-H2BeGFP reporter is clearly expressed in the neural plate at HH5 and later in the neural fold/tube including the dorsal portion.
source: The reporter is clearly expressed in the neural plate at HH5 and later in the neural fold/tube including the dorsal portion (Figure 5A) as expected and previously described (Uchikawa et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5A and citation to previous work.

claim: Enhancer-driven H2BeGFP expression remains in the migrating neural crest as well as a few epidermal cells at HH12.
source: In addition, we find that enhancer-driven H2BeGFP expression remains in the migrating neural crest as well as a few epidermal cells at HH12 and that signal is even detectable as late as HH14 (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 5A and 5B.

claim: N1N2-H2BeGFP signal is detectable as late as HH14.
source: In addition, we find that enhancer-driven H2BeGFP expression remains in the migrating neural crest as well as a few epidermal cells at HH12 and that signal is even detectable as late as HH14 (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Time-lapse imaging reveals streams of N1N2-H2BeGFP expressing neural crest cells emerging from the dorsal neural tube and migrating into the facial region.
source: To follow Sox2 expressing cells as function of time in live embryos, we performed time-lapse imaging to visualize the movement of cells expressing the Sox2 reporter. The results reveal streams of N1N2-H2BeGFP expressing neural crest cells emerging from the dorsal neural tube (Video 1) and migrating into the facial region.
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Video 1.

claim: Migrating neural crest cells are observed after electroporation of the N1N2 Sox2-H2B-eGFP reporter at HH7 (2ss) and HH8 (4ss).
source: We targeted the closing neural tube at HH7 (2ss) to HH8 (4ss) in ovo, reflecting stages just before and after neural tube closure, respectively. Interestingly, we observe migrating neural crest cells that expressed the eGFP reporter after electroportion at both stages (Figure 5C,D), indicating that cells continue to produce eGFP protein under control of these neural enhancers until time points just before neural crest migration initiates.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 5C and D.

claim: Cells continue to produce eGFP protein under control of the N1N2 neural enhancers until time points just before neural crest migration initiates.
source: We targeted the closing neural tube at HH7 (2ss) to HH8 (4ss) in ovo, reflecting stages just before and after neural tube closure, respectively. Interestingly, we observe migrating neural crest cells that expressed the eGFP reporter after electroportion at both stages (Figure 5C,D), indicating that cells continue to produce eGFP protein under control of these neural enhancers until time points just before neural crest migration initiates.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data shown in Figures 5C and D.

claim: The Pest domain has been reported to reduce the half-life of GFP to 9.8 hr in mammalian cells.
source: The Pest domain has been reported to reduce the half-life of GFP to 9.8 hr in mammalian cells (Corish and Tyler-Smith, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: After electroporation of the destabilized Sox2-reporter (N1N2-eGFP-Pest), only a very low level of enhancer driven eGFP expression is observed in the dorsal neural tube.
source: After electroporation of the destabilized Sox2-reporter, we observe only a very low level of enhancer driven eGFP expression in the dorsal neural tube (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The N1N2-eGFP-Pest reporter is not detectable in migrating neural crest cells, whereas low levels of Sox2 protein expression remain.
source: Consistent with this, the N1N2-reporter is not detectable in migrating neural crest cells, whereas low levels of Sox2 protein expression remain (Figure 5E', arrowheads).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5E'.

claim: Sox2 protein expression in neural crest cells perdures from transcription and translation occurring prior to migration rather than being newly produced.
source: This indicates that Sox2 protein expression in neural crest cells perdures from transcription and translation occurring prior to migration rather than being newly produced.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the destabilized reporter data.

claim: At HH7 and HH8, strong Sox2 mRNA is observed in the neural plate border and dorsal neural folds with complete overlap with the Pax7 protein expression domain.
source: At HH7 and HH8 (Figure 5F,G) we observe strong Sox2 mRNA in the neural plate border and dorsal neural folds and complete overlap with the Pax7 protein expression domain as detected by immunostaining after in situ hybridization.
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figures 5F and G.

claim: At HH9 Sox2 mRNA expression in the dorsal neural tube is greatly reduced to almost undetectable levels.
source: At HH9 Sox2 mRNA expression in the dorsal neural tube is greatly reduced to almost undetectable levels (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: The drop of Sox2 mRNA expression between HH8 and HH9 is consistent with the decline of Sox2 protein at that stage although it remains detectable.
source: This drop of Sox2 mRNA expression between HH8 and HH9 is consistent with the decline of Sox2 protein at that stage (Figure 3J) although it remains detectable.
evidence: This is an interpretation comparing mRNA and protein data.

claim: At HH13, Sox2 mRNA is no longer seen in the dorsal neural tube, whereas Sox2 protein is still present in that region likely due to protein stability after Sox2 mRNA is degraded.
source: At HH13 we no longer see Sox2 transcripts in the dorsal neural tube (Figure 5I'), whereas Sox2 protein is still present in that region likely due to protein stability after Sox2 mRNA is degraded.
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 5I' and includes an interpretation about protein stability.

claim: Sox2 mRNA expression is barely detectable in migrating neural crest as it can only be observed at very low levels in the rhombomere 4 stream (pre-otic level) where the neural crest population is very dense.
source: Sox2 mRNA expression is barely detectable in migrating neural crest as it can only be observed at very low levels in the rhombomere 4 stream (pre-otic level) where the neural crest population is very dense (Figure 5I'').
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 5I''.

claim: At HH6, Msx1 mRNA expression is nested within the Pax7 protein expression domain.
source: ISH also reveals overlap of Pax7 and the neural plate border markers Msx1 and Tfap2a at mRNA level. At HH6 we see Msx1 mRNA expression nested within the Pax7 protein expression domain (Figure 5J).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 5J.

claim: At HH9 Msx1 mRNA expression overlaps with Pax7 protein expression in the dorsal neural tube and the delaminated neural crest.
source: At HH9 Msx1 mRNA expression overlaps with Pax7 protein expression in the dorsal neural tube and the delaminated neural crest.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the in situ hybridization data.

claim: Tfap2a mRNA expression overlaps with Pax7 protein expression in the dorsal neural fold at HH8.
source: Similarly, Tfap2a mRNA expression overlaps with Pax7 protein expression in the dorsal neural fold at HH8 (Figure 5L).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 5L.

claim: Overexpression of Sox2 in the neural plate border results in a significant decrease in Pax7 expression.
source: The results show that overexpression of Sox2 in the neural plate border results in a significant decrease in Pax7 expression (Figure 6C,D,E), in contrast to control embryos (Figure 6A,B and E).
evidence: This is supported by gain-of-function experimental data shown in Figures 6C-E.

claim: The decrease in Pax7 expression upon Sox2 overexpression seems to be cell autonomous since cells expressing a high level of Sox2 in the dorsal neural fold have greatly reduced Pax7 expression.
source: This seems to be cell autonomous since cells expressing a high level of Sox2 in the dorsal neural fold have greatly reduced Pax7 expression (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6F and is an interpretation of the cell-level observations.

claim: Sox2 knockdown with morpholino resulted in a small but statistically significant decrease in Sox2 protein levels that caused a statistically significant increase of Pax7 protein expression.
source: To this end, we electroporated one side of HH4 chicken embryos with a Sox2 translation-blocking morpholino (MO) and the other side with a control morpholino at a concentration of 0.5 mM. This resulted in a small but statistically significant decrease in Sox2 protein levels that in turn caused a statistically significant increase of Pax7 protein expression (5–11 sections/embryo, n = 9) (Figure 6G,H).
evidence: This is supported by loss-of-function experimental data shown in Figures 6G and H.

claim: Co-electroporation of Sox2 MO with pCaggs-Sox2 resulted in marked rescue of the loss-of-function phenotype, restoring Pax7 expression.
source: To control for the specificity of Sox2 MO and to demonstrate that the observed phenotype was not due to off-target binding, we co-electroporated the Sox2 MO with pCaggs-Sox2 (4–7 sections/embryo, n = 16 embryos). This resulted in marked rescue of the loss-of-function phenotype, restoring Pax7 expression (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: In about half of the embryos, Sox10 and FoxD3 mRNA expression levels are increased on the Sox2 MO electroporated side when compared to the control MO treated side.
source: To investigate if a decrease in Sox2 expression leads to fate changes at later stages, we again electroporated HH4 embryos with control MO and Sox2 MO on left and right side, respectively, and performed ISH for the neural crest markers Sox10 (n = 26 embryos) and FoxD3 (n = 14 embryos). We see that in about half of the embryos Sox10 and FoxD3 mRNA expression levels are increased on the Sox2 MO electroporated side when compared to the control MO treated side (Figure 6I–K), suggesting a change in fate.
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figures 6I-K.

claim: Overexpression of Pax7 resulted in a small, but significant decrease in Sox2 protein expression when compared to the untreated control side of the embryo.
source: Similar to the experiment above, we overexpressed Pax7 using pCI-Pax7-IRES-H2B-RFP which resulted in a small, but significant decrease in Sox2 protein expression (Figure 7B–D) when compared to the untreated control side of the embryo (3–6 sections/embryo, n = 8 embryos).
evidence: This is supported by gain-of-function experimental data shown in Figures 7B-D.

claim: When compared to control embryos electroporated with the empty vector pCI-H2B-RFP, the difference in Sox2 expression upon Pax7 overexpression was not statistically significant.
source: However, when compared to control embryos electroporated with the empty vector pCI-H2B-RFP (3–6 sections/embryo, n = 7 embryos) (Figure 7A,C and D), the difference was not statistically significant.
evidence: This is supported by comparison to control data shown in Figures 7A, C, and D.

claim: Single cell analysis shows that the Pax7-H2B-RFP treated side had a statistically significant decrease of Sox2 protein expression in cells with very strong RFP expression when compared to the control side.
source: Using Fiji software, we measured the intensity of Sox2 and Pax7 expression in cells with very strong RFP expression in embryos that were injected with Pax7-H2B-RFP on the one side and H2B-RFP on the other side (Figure 7E). As expected, cells expressing high levels of RFP also express high levels of Pax7 on the Pax7-H2B-RFP treated side (total of 44 cells of 5 embryos, 2–6 sections evaluated per embryo) but not on the H2B-RFP control side (total of 35 cells of 5 embryos, 4–6 sections evaluated per embryo) (Figure 7F). The Pax7-H2B-RFP treated side also had a statistically significant decrease of Sox2 protein expression in these cells when compared to the control side (Figure 7G).
evidence: This is supported by single cell quantitative analysis shown in Figures 7E-G.

claim: The decrease in Sox2 upon Pax7 overexpression indicates a cell autonomous function for Pax7.
source: This indicates a cell autonomous function for Pax7.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the single cell analysis data.

claim: Pax7 knockdown with morpholino resulted in downregulation of Pax7 protein which caused a significant increase in Sox2 protein expression.
source: In the reciprocal experiment for loss of Pax7, one side of HH4 embryos was electroporated with a Pax7 MO (Basch et al., 2006; Simões-Costa et al., 2012) and the other side with control morpholino (Figure 7H). This resulted in downregulation of Pax7 protein on the Pax7-MO electroporated side after Pax7 immunostaining which in turn caused a significant increase in Sox2 protein expression (5–10 sections/embryo, n = 14 embryos) (Figure 7I).
evidence: This is supported by loss-of-function experimental data shown in Figures 7H and I.

claim: When performing ISH for Sox10 mRNA in Pax7 MO treated embryos, Sox10 reduction is seen on the Pax7 MO treated side.
source: When performing ISH for Sox10 mRNA in MO treated embryos (n = 9 embryos), we see Sox10 reduction on the Pax7 MO treated side (Figure 7J–L), as shown previously at a higher Pax7 MO concentration (Basch et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figures 7J-L and citation to previous work.

claim: There is a reciprocal relationship between levels of Sox2 and Pax7.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that there is a reciprocal relationship between levels of Sox2 and Pax7 and that altering these levels affects the balance between prospective neural tube versus neural crest cell fates.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the combined gain- and loss-of-function experiments.

claim: Altering Sox2 and Pax7 levels affects the balance between prospective neural tube versus neural crest cell fates.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that there is a reciprocal relationship between levels of Sox2 and Pax7 and that altering these levels affects the balance between prospective neural tube versus neural crest cell fates.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the combined gain- and loss-of-function experiments.

claim: Neural plate border cells can be biased to a different fate by relatively small changes in transcription factor levels.
source: This suggests that neural plate border cells can be biased to a different fate by relatively small changes in transcription factor levels.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results showing that modulating Sox2 and Pax7 levels affects cell fate.

claim: Transcriptional priming, or the expression of numerous mixed-lineage-affiliated programs, has been described extensively during stem cell fate determination in the hematopoietic system.
source: Transition of a stem cell into a specialized state often involves several cell fate decisions. Transcriptional priming, or the expression of numerous mixed-lineage-affiliated programs, has been described extensively during stem cell fate determination in the hematopoietic system (Hu et al., 1997; Laslo et al., 2006; Olsson et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies in the hematopoietic system.

claim: Mixed-lineage states are generally achieved by expression of alternative lineage determinants like transcription factors and have been proposed to be mandatory steps in cell fate specification.
source: These mixed-lineage states are generally achieved by expression of alternative lineage determinants like transcription factors and have been proposed to be mandatory steps in cell fate specification.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field of stem cell biology.

claim: Single-cell analysis of primary chicken erythroid progenitors revealed a peak of high cell-to-cell variability in gene expression that precedes an irreversible commitment to differentiation, before being strongly decreased.
source: Additionally, single-cell analysis of primary chicken erythroid progenitors revealed a peak of high cell-to-cell variability in gene expression, that precedes an irreversible commitment to differentiation, before being strongly decreased (Richard et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: A similar transcriptional priming appears to occur in the neural plate border.
source: Here we show that a similar transcriptional priming appears to occur in the neural plate border, which contains precursors of neural, neural crest, placodal and epidermal cells.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the Discussion, drawing a parallel to hematopoietic stem cells.

claim: Previous studies have examined gene expression at the neural plate border by in situ hybridization but the resolution was not sufficient to resolve whether there are characteristic subdomains of cells fated toward neural crest, ectodermal placode, neural or epidermal fates.
source: Although previous studies have examined gene expression at the neural plate border by in situ hybridization (Khudyakov and Bronner-Fraser, 2009; Streit and Stern, 1999), the resolution was not sufficient to resolve whether there are characteristic subdomains of cells fated toward neural crest, ectodermal placode, neural or epidermal fates.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies and identifies a limitation of those studies.

claim: The neural plate border region is not comprised of separate zones containing prospective placodal, neural and neural crest, but rather contains a mixture of intermingled precursors which are not fate-restricted.
source: Our results show that individual neural plate border cells have a high degree of overlap of multiple markers even at early gastrula stages. This overlap is maintained within the rising neural folds until the time of neural tube closure and in some migrating neural crest cells. This suggests that the neural plate border region is not comprised of separate zones containing prospective placodal, neural and neural crest, but rather contains a mixture of intermingled precursors which are not fate-restricted.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Initially naïve cells are open to many possible fates and retain the ability to contribute to multiple lineages ranging from neural crest, placodal, epidermal and central nervous system fates.
source: Consistent with flexibility of cell fates, explant experiments have shown that intermediate neural plate tissue, normally fated to form CNS, can give rise to neural crest cells when exposed to BMP signaling in culture (Liem et al., 1995). Thus, we speculate that initially naïve cells are open to many possible fates and retain the ability to contribute to multiple lineages ranging from neural crest, placodal, epidermal and central nervous system fates.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion supported by the current data and citation to previous explant experiments.

claim: Explant experiments have shown that intermediate neural plate tissue, normally fated to form CNS, can give rise to neural crest cells when exposed to BMP signaling in culture.
source: Consistent with flexibility of cell fates, explant experiments have shown that intermediate neural plate tissue, normally fated to form CNS, can give rise to neural crest cells when exposed to BMP signaling in culture (Liem et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Stochastic gene expression may account for variation in cell to cell protein expression.
source: For example, Pax7 alone was seen in 12–26% of neural plate border cells, Sox2 between 13–24% and Six1 from 1–3% of cells at any particular stage. Although this may indicate commitment to a particular lineage, it is equally possible that stochastic gene expression accounts for this variation in cell to cell protein expression (Elowitz et al., 2002; McAdams and Arkin, 1997).
evidence: This is a possible explanation supported by citations to previous studies on stochastic gene expression.

claim: The number of cells expressing single markers did not increase as a function of time, as might be expected with progressive commitment toward a particular fate, but rather dropped.
source: It is interesting to note that the number of cells expressing single markers did not increase as a function of time, as might be expected with progressive commitment toward a particular fate, but rather dropped.
evidence: This is an observation from the quantitative data that contradicts expectations of progressive fate restriction.

claim: Single cells that concomitantly expressed multiple markers were much more prevalent than those expressing a single factor.
source: Furthermore, single cells that concomitantly expressed multiple markers were much more prevalent than those expressing a single factor.
evidence: This is a summary of the quantitative data presented in the Results section.

claim: The majority of neural plate border cells are open to multiple fates.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that the majority of neural plate border cells are open to multiple fates.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined experimental data.

claim: Six1 expression is primarily in the lateral portions of the neural plate border and Pax7 expression is biased toward the medial regions.
source: Classical descriptions of the vertebrate neural plate border at neurula stages draw different domains within the border region, with placodal precursors populating a more lateral domain and neural crest precursors a more medial domain. Consistent with this view, we see Six1 expression primarily in the lateral portions of the neural plate border and Pax7 expression biased toward the medial regions.
evidence: This is supported by the spatial distribution analysis presented in the Results section.

claim: No sharp demarcations exist between precursor populations and extensive intermixing is observed such that even cells expressing a single marker were adjacent to border cells expressing multiple markers.
source: However, no sharp demarcations exist between precursor populations and we noted extensive intermixing such that even cells expressing a single marker were adjacent to border cells expressing multiple markers.
evidence: This is an observation from the immunostaining and spatial distribution data.

claim: Explants of the prospective neural plate border at a late blastula stage (HH2) were found to express neural, neural crest, epidermal and to a small extent placode markers.
source: These results are consistent with explant studies performed in mouse embryos. Explants of the prospective neural plate border at a late blastula stage (HH2) were found to express neural, neural crest, epidermal and to a small extent placode markers (Patthey et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous explant study in mouse.

claim: The idea of distinct precursor subdomains within the vertebrate neural plate border cannot be substantiated.
source: In agreement with these findings, we conclude that the idea of distinct precursor subdomains within the vertebrate neural plate border cannot be substantiated.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the current data and comparison to previous studies.

claim: In contrast to the chick neural plate border region, neural and epidermal fates in basal invertebrate chordates such as amphioxus are separated by a sharp border.
source: In contrast to the chick neural plate border region, neural and epidermal fates in basal invertebrate chordates such as amphioxus are separated by a sharp border.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about basal chordates.

claim: Urochordates have an invariant cell lineage such that the fate of neural versus epidermal precursors is fixed prior to the gastrula stages.
source: Even urochordates have an invariant cell lineage such that the fate of neural versus epidermal precursors is fixed prior to the gastrula stages (Conklin, 1905; Lemaire, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on urochordate development.

claim: The caudal neural plate border of Ciona intestinalis contains a precursor to bipolar tail neuron (BTNs) that delaminates and migrates along the paraxial mesoderm on either side of the neural tube.
source: However, recent evidence has shown that the caudal neural plate border of Ciona intestinalis contains a precursor to bipolar tail neuron (BTNs) (Stolfi et al., 2015) that delaminates and migrates along the paraxial mesoderm on either side of the neural tube.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a recent study on Ciona.

claim: BTN precursors in Ciona share some properties as well as some molecular markers with vertebrate neural crest cells, including co-expression of neural plate border and neural crest markers like Msx and Snail.
source: These cells share some properties as well as some molecular markers with vertebrate neural crest cells, including co-expression of neural plate border and neural crest markers like Msx and Snail.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the cited Ciona study.

claim: An intriguing possibility is that advent of neural crest and placode cells in the vertebrate lineage resulted in the superposition of a multifated neural plate border region onto a sharp neural/epidermal border in the chordate ancestor.
source: Thus, an intriguing possibility is that advent of neural crest and placode cells in the vertebrate lineage resulted in the superposition of a multifated neural plate border region onto a sharp neural/epidermal border in the chordate ancestor and that urochordates may already possess an 'intermediate' neural plate border with partial overlap of marker expression.
evidence: This is a speculative evolutionary interpretation based on comparisons between vertebrates and basal chordates.

claim: Urochordates may already possess an 'intermediate' neural plate border with partial overlap of marker expression.
source: Thus, an intriguing possibility is that advent of neural crest and placode cells in the vertebrate lineage resulted in the superposition of a multifated neural plate border region onto a sharp neural/epidermal border in the chordate ancestor and that urochordates may already possess an 'intermediate' neural plate border with partial overlap of marker expression.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the Ciona data.

claim: Previous single cell lineage analyses in chick trunk have shown that individual dorsal neural tube cells are multipotent and able to contribute to both neural crest and dorsal neural tube.
source: Accordingly, previous single cell lineage analyses in chick (Bronner-Fraser and Fraser, 1988; McKinney et al., 2013) and mouse (Baggiolini et al., 2015) trunk have shown that individual dorsal neural tube cells are multipotent and able to contribute to both neural crest and dorsal neural tube.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous single cell lineage tracing studies.

claim: Previous single cell lineage analyses in mouse trunk have shown that individual dorsal neural tube cells are multipotent and able to contribute to both neural crest and dorsal neural tube.
source: Accordingly, previous single cell lineage analyses in chick (Bronner-Fraser and Fraser, 1988; McKinney et al., 2013) and mouse (Baggiolini et al., 2015) trunk have shown that individual dorsal neural tube cells are multipotent and able to contribute to both neural crest and dorsal neural tube.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous single cell lineage tracing studies.

claim: Small changes in transcription factor levels can bias cells toward a particular lineage.
source: Consistent with these lineage studies, our data suggest that the majority of neural plate border cells in vertebrate embryos are open to numerous prospective fates. We further suggest that small changes in transcription factor levels can bias cells toward a particular lineage.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the gain- and loss-of-function experiments.

claim: Subtle modulations of either Sox2 or Pax7 levels can shift the balance of neural versus neural crest cells.
source: For example, we find that subtle modulations of either Sox2 or Pax7 levels can shift the balance of neural versus neural crest cells.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data from gain- and loss-of-function experiments.

claim: In Drosophila, mutually repressive transcription factors regulate each other's relative expression, leading to sharp segmental borders.
source: This is similar to the well-known Drosophila gap gene scenario where mutually repressive transcription factors regulate each other's relative expression, leading to sharp segmental borders (Jäckle et al., 1986; Jaeger, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on Drosophila gap genes.

claim: During patterning of the vertebrate neural tube, a transcriptional network of three transcription factors (Pax6, Olig2 and Nkx2.2) defines the final positions of the boundaries of distinct ventral progenitor domains.
source: During patterning of the vertebrate neural tube, a transcriptional network of three transcription factors (Pax6, Olig2 and Nkx2.2) defines the final positions of the boundaries of distinct ventral progenitor domains (Briscoe et al., 2000, 1999; Ericson et al., 1997; Novitch et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on neural tube patterning.

claim: The three transcription factor circuit (Pax6, Olig2 and Nkx2.2) encodes a multistable switch that results in stabilizing neural tube patterning.
source: It was proposed that this three transcription factor circuit encodes a multistable switch that results in stabilizing neural tube patterning (Balaskas et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The mutual repression of Sox2 and Pax7 can lead to a bistable switch with three solutions.
source: Similarly, we propose that the mutual repression of Sox2 and Pax7 can lead to a bistable switch with three solutions (Figure 8): an unstable state occurs when the concentration of two cross-repressing factors is similar.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the experimental data, illustrated in Figure 8.

claim: According to the bistable switch model, increase of Sox2 expression above a certain threshold represses expression of Pax7 that in turn leads to neural fate.
source: According to this model, increase of Sox2 expression above a certain threshold represses expression of Pax7 that in turn leads to neural fate.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model based on the experimental data.

claim: According to the bistable switch model, high levels of Pax7 induce reduction of Sox2 in the dorsal neural fold and lead to a neural crest fate.
source: In the reciprocal situation, high levels of Pax7 induce reduction of Sox2 in the dorsal neural fold and lead to a neural crest fate.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model based on the experimental data.

claim: In Xenopus, high levels of the placodal genes Eya1 and Six1 promote proliferation of placodal neuronal progenitor by modulating SoxB1 expression, while lower levels promote neuronal differentiation.
source: In Xenopus a similar model has been proposed for protein cross-regulation during cranial ganglion neurogenesis. This work shows that high levels of the placodal genes Eya1 and Six1 promote proliferation of placodal neuronal progenitor by modulating SoxB1 expression, while lower levels promote neuronal differentiation (Schlosser et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study in Xenopus.

claim: Dlx proteins have been shown to shift the position of the zebrafish neural plate border causing changes of cell fates in that region.
source: For instance, Dlx proteins have been shown to shift the position of the zebrafish neural plate border causing changes of cell fates in that region (Woda et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study in zebrafish.

claim: By inhibiting or ectopically activating endogenous Dlx protein, an expansion of the neural plate into the non-neural ectoderm or reduction of neural differentiation is observed, respectively.
source: By inhibiting or ectopically activating endogenous Dlx protein, these authors observed an expansion of the neural plate into the non-neural ectoderm or reduction of neural differentiation, respectively.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the cited zebrafish study.

claim: Altering BMP levels in frog and chick embryos shifts the position of the neural plate border.
source: Similarly, altering BMP levels in frog and chick embryos shifts the position of the neural plate border (Marchant et al., 1998; Streit and Stern, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies in frog and chick.

claim: Overexpression of Sox2 in the neural folds causes down-regulation of neural crest specifier genes FoxD3, Snail2 and Sox10.
source: Overexpression of Sox2 in the neural folds causes down-regulation of neural crest specifier genes FoxD3, Snail2 and Sox10 (Hu et al., 2012; Wakamatsu et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The neural plate border region appears to be highly regulative in ability to respond to transcriptional modifications.
source: Thus, the neural plate border region appears to be highly regulative in ability to respond to transcriptional modifications.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the various examples of transcription factor manipulations affecting the neural plate border.

claim: The neural plate border contains precursors which have mixed identity until at least the time of neural tube closure.
source: In summary, our data show that the neural plate border contains precursors which have mixed identity until at least the time of neural tube closure.
evidence: This is the main conclusion summarizing the findings of the study.

claim: Correct timing of cell fate decisions and differentiation is important for proper embryonic development, stem cell biology, regenerative medicine and cancer cell biology.
source: These findings have implications for several fields of biology as correct timing of cell fate decisions and differentiation is not only important for proper embryonic development, but also for stem cell biology, regenerative medicine and cancer cell biology, where new protocols are needed for cell specification and to understand why cells dedifferentiate to return to a progenitor state.
evidence: This is stated as the broader implications of the findings.
